author: Eusebius of Caesarea
note: The Papias tradition on the origin of Mark's Gospel. This is a chain of testimony: Eusebius (c. 325) quotes Papias of Hierapolis (writing c. 95–110), who in turn reports what 'the presbyter' (traditionally John the Elder) said. It is the earliest external witness that Mark wrote from Peter's preaching — apologetically load-bearing for the Gospel-as-eyewitness-derived case. Store as historical testimony, not as proof; note that 'not in order' is Papias's own qualification and that scholars debate whether 'the presbyter' is John the apostle or a distinct John the Elder. Verified verbatim vs source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-11).
text: This also the presbyter said: Mark, having become the interpreter of Peter, wrote down accurately, though not in order, whatsoever he remembered of the things said or done by Christ. For he neither heard the Lord nor followed him, but afterward, as I said, he followed Peter, who adapted his teaching to the needs of his hearers, but with no intention of giving a connected account of the Lord's discourses, so that Mark committed no error while he thus wrote some things as he remembered them. For he was careful of one thing, not to omit any of the things which he had heard, and not to state any of them falsely.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea
note: The Papias tradition on Matthew — the earliest external statement that Matthew composed the 'oracles' (logia) in the Hebrew (i.e. Hebrew/Aramaic) tongue. Store as historical testimony via Eusebius (c. 325) quoting Papias (c. 95–110). Handle with care in essays: 'the oracles' (ta logia) and 'in the Hebrew language' are scholarly cruxes — it is debated whether Papias means our Greek Matthew, an Aramaic sayings-source, or a Hebrew style of composition. Do not overstate it as a simple proof of Matthean authorship of canonical Greek Matthew. Verified verbatim vs source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-11).
text: So then Matthew wrote the oracles in the Hebrew language, and every one interpreted them as he was able.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea
note: Eusebius's summary of the 'acknowledged' (homologoumena) New Testament writings, c. 325 — the four Gospels, Acts, Paul's epistles, 1 John, 1 Peter, and (with a noted reservation) Revelation. Apologetically useful for showing a settled core canon early in the fourth century. Store with the accurate qualifier: Eusebius classes these as the recognized books, but immediately proceeds to list 'disputed' (antilegomena) and 'rejected' books — so quote this as evidence for the stable CORE, not as a claim that the full 27-book canon was undebated. His own hesitation over the Apocalypse ('if it really seem proper') should be represented, not smoothed over. Verified verbatim vs source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-11).
text: Since we are dealing with this subject it is proper to sum up the writings of the New Testament which have been already mentioned. First then must be put the holy quaternion of the Gospels; following them the Acts of the Apostles. After this must be reckoned the epistles of Paul; next in order the extant former epistle of John, and likewise the epistle of Peter, must be maintained. After them is to be placed, if it really seem proper, the Apocalypse of John, concerning which we shall give the different opinions at the proper time. These then belong among the accepted writings.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea
note: IMPORTANT / handle with care. Eusebius here attributes to Josephus a saying that the fall of Jerusalem avenged the murder of James the Just, 'a brother of Jesus, that is called the Christ.' This exact sentence is NOT found in the surviving manuscripts of Josephus; both Eusebius and (earlier) Origen cite it, but scholars regard it as a non-genuine addition — it is not the authentic James reference. The genuine, widely-accepted Josephus notice of James is Antiquities 20.9.1 (20.200): 'the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, whose name was James.' A future essay should cite the authentic Antiquities 20.200 passage for the historical James, and use THIS Eusebian quotation only as evidence of early Christian tradition ABOUT Josephus — never present it as Josephus's own verified words. Related caution: Eusebius's fuller Josephus 'Testimonium Flavianum' (HE 1.11 / Antiquities 18.3.3) is widely regarded as containing later Christian interpolation and must be quoted only in a carefully qualified form. Verified verbatim vs source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-11).
text: Josephus, at least, has not hesitated to testify this in his writings, where he says, 'These things happened to the Jews to avenge James the Just, who was a brother of Jesus, that is called the Christ. For the Jews slew him, although he was a most just man.'

author: Eusebius of Caesarea
note: Polycarp of Smyrna's reply to the proconsul, quoted by Eusebius (c. 325) from the letter of the church of Smyrna (the Martyrdom of Polycarp, c. 155–160). A short, vivid witness to the steadfastness of the martyrs — apologetically useful as evidence of sincere conviction unto death, not as independent proof of any doctrinal claim. Store as historical testimony; note that Eusebius is quoting an earlier document, and that 'eighty-six years' likely dates Polycarp's Christian life, not simply his age. Verified verbatim vs source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-11).
text: But when the magistrate pressed him, and said, 'Swear, and I will release thee; revile Christ,' Polycarp said, 'Fourscore and six years have I been serving him, and he hath done me no wrong; how then can I blaspheme my king who saved me?'

author: Phileas of Thmuis (quoted in Eusebius of Caesarea)
work: Letter of Phileas, in Eusebius, Church History
note: A first-person witness from inside the Great Persecution (c. AD 303-311). Phileas, bishop of Thmuis in Egypt, wrote this letter to his church from prison in Alexandria shortly before his own martyrdom (c. 306); Eusebius quotes it at length in Church History VIII.10. In this sentence the presiding judge orders the officers torturing the martyrs to pay them no attention at all - to act as if the sufferers no longer existed - which Phileas names a second torture added to the physical stripes. Store as historical testimony to how the persecution sought to un-person its victims, not as doctrinal proof. Wording verified byte-for-byte against the source_url (and Wikisource) by apologia-citations, 2026-08-25; the clause “were to think and act as if we no longer existed” is McGiffert’s actual translation, not a paraphrase. Do NOT re-attribute this exact wording to the ANF vol. 6 Roberts-Donaldson Phileas fragment - that is a different translation.
text: For he said that they were not to have the least concern for us, but were to think and act as if we no longer existed, our enemies having invented this second mode of torture in addition to the stripes.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea
section: Bk V.28.5 (quoting the anonymous anti-Artemon work, the 'Little Labyrinth')
note: From an anonymous early-third-century work (the 'Little Labyrinth', attributed to Hippolytus of Rome or to Gaius, c. AD 230-240), quoted by Eusebius, refuting the Artemonites' claim that the deity of Christ was a recent corruption of an originally 'mere man' teaching. The writer appeals to the church's hymnody 'from the beginning' as evidence that Christ was praised as God long before Nicaea - load-bearing against the 'Nicaea/Constantine invented Jesus' divinity' claim. A chain of testimony: Eusebius (c. 325) quotes the anonymous writer (c. 230-240) reporting hymnody 'from the beginning'. Store as historical testimony to early Christian worship of Christ, not as proof of the doctrine itself. Verified verbatim vs source_url (web, 2026-10-05).
text: And how many psalms and hymns, written by the faithful brethren from the beginning, celebrate Christ the Word of God, speaking of him as Divine.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea
note: Origen (as quoted by Eusebius) on the Epistle to the Hebrews: its author is unknown, and earlier writers had credited it to Clement of Rome or to Luke. This is the contrast case for the Gospels. A genuinely nameless early Christian text drew several rival attributions (here Clement and Luke; Paul in EH 6.14.2; Barnabas in Tertullian, On Modesty 20), while the early sources show no rival tradition of authorship for the Gospels (on the disputed Cerinthus report see library/eyewitnesses.html n. 20). That is an argument from silence; label it so wherever it is used. Added 2026-11-15 from the Gathercole anonymity mine (backlog GATH-5); text copied from source_url. Verified verbatim vs source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-11-15).
text: But who wrote the epistle, in truth, God knows. The statement of some who have gone before us is that Clement, bishop of the Romans, wrote the epistle, and of others that Luke, the author of the Gospel and the Acts, wrote it.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea
note: Clement of Alexandria (c. 200, via Eusebius) credits Hebrews to Paul, with Luke as its translator. It is one of the several rival attributions of the nameless Hebrews; see eusebius-he-6-25-14 for the contrast with the Gospels. Added 2026-11-15 from the Gathercole anonymity mine (backlog GATH-5); text copied from source_url. Verified verbatim vs source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-11-15).
text: He says that the Epistle to the Hebrews is the work of Paul, and that it was written to the Hebrews in the Hebrew language; but that Luke translated it carefully and published it for the Greeks, and hence the same style of expression is found in this epistle and in the Acts.

author: Eusebius of Caesarea
note: Polycrates of Ephesus (190s, letter to Victor of Rome, via Eusebius) identifies a John buried at Ephesus as the one 'who reclined upon the bosom of the Lord', i.e. the Beloved Disciple of John 13:23-25. Bauckham argues this John is NOT the son of Zebedee but Papias's 'John the Elder'. Use it only for the early identification of the Beloved Disciple as a John; it does not settle WHICH John. Added 2026-11-15 from the Gathercole anonymity mine (backlog GATH-5); text copied from source_url. Verified verbatim vs source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-11-15).
text: Among these are Philip, one of the twelve apostles, who fell asleep in Hierapolis; and his two aged virgin daughters, and another daughter, who lived in the Holy Spirit and now rests at Ephesus; and, moreover, John, who was both a witness and a teacher, who reclined upon the bosom of the Lord, and, being a priest, wore the sacerdotal plate.
